name: Anthropomorphism in House Façades – Adjectives and 12 Statements
description: Faithful replication with the paper's own stimuli: Weber, Roessler, Riebandt & Kühn (2024), "Predictors of explicit and implicit anthropomorphism in house facades", Scientific Reports 14: 28291. The stimuli are 50 photographs from the DalHouses set (Filliter et al. 2016, figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.1279430, CC BY 4.0), the set the paper used. Part 1 (implicit measure): for each house, in random order, participants complete “This house is …” and “This house makes me …” with the adjectives that come to mind. Part 2 (explicit measure): each house is shown again in a new random order with 12 statements rated on 0–100 sliders (not applicable at all to very applicable): the house has a face, is typical, looks familiar, childlike, inviting, friendly, I like it, I would feel safe, it looks threatening, I would feel lonely, I would feel free, I would like to live with others in it. Age, gender and country are asked at the end. Answers are keyed by DalHouse number. In the paper (305 participants in Germany, Denmark and Canada), the same houses scored highest on 7 of the 12 statements in all three countries, and explicit anthropomorphism fell with age. Differences from the original study: (1) the paper chose 50 of the 100 DalHouses by sorting on mean face-likeness and taking every other house but does not list them; this template sorts the published DalHouse face-likeness ratings and takes ranks 1, 3, 5 … 99, so the set may differ slightly; (2) the 9-item short IDAQ (individual differences in anthropomorphism) is not included; (3) runs in English only (the paper also used a German version); (4) demographics are reduced to age, gender and country.
author: Weber, Roessler, Riebandt & Kühn

config.description: Participants first complete two sentences about each of 50 house façades (“This house is …”, “This house makes me …”) and then rate every façade on 12 statements (face-likeness, typicality, familiarity, childlikeness, invitingness, friendliness, liking, safety, threat, loneliness, freedom, living with others) with 0–100 sliders. Rebuilt from Weber, Roessler, Riebandt & Kühn (2024), Scientific Reports 14: 28291, with the 50 DalHouses photographs (Filliter et al. 2016, figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.1279430, CC BY 4.0).
